title: Hot-take with Boz on frontier vs open models
power_dynamic: senior engineer-executive peer, external, blunt. Combative but fair, owns his own bias out loud, zero tolerance for opinions formed without doing the work. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Alright, give me your real take. Frontier models or open weights for what you're building, where do you actually land? And don't give me the both-have-tradeoffs answer.

What I'm building is a job, and the thing that needs to be done is much more specific and concrete. Pushing for frontier capabilities is not needed, and frontier capabilities are improving with different resources and different costs. For the voice agent, the one I have is much more specific, and from a budget and economics perspective, the open weights one works much better. That's what we're doing.

I can get in the head of someone who picks open weights for a voice agent. You're optimizing for predictable cost and you know your domain well enough to trim the fat. The problem is you're trading compute you can measure for labor you can't. Who tunes that thing when the edge cases stack up, and what's your actual ceiling on call quality?

You have hardness and evals to tune the whole thing, right? It's not just about the models. It's the hardness, the setup, the evaluations, and going back and configuring that. Even open weights here means I'm using an inference provider. I'm not looking through the lake of hosting it locally.

So you're not even running the weights. You're paying an inference provider for what is effectively a proprietary API with extra steps. The latency point is real, but the cost math is where you lose me. What happens when that provider changes their pricing or their model card, and your whole eval suite was tuned to the old logits?

Your hardware and eval are the crux of things. It does have a few reconfigurations, and you can swap the eval sets with a new model. That optionality is always a thing. There is always a risk, and you need to be ready with replacements.

Have you actually run that swap, or is that a thing you read? I've seen teams burn six weeks re-tuning a pipeline because the new model's tokenizer changed the batch boundaries. The optionality exists on paper. In practice, you pay in labor for what you saved in compute.
I meant hardness and revals, not hardware.

Fair. Hardness and evals is the right frame. But you just described a plan that works until it doesn't. You're betting the provider keeps backward compatibility. I'd bet they break it to ship faster. Have you actually run the swap on this specific agent, or is that a hypothetical you're comfortable with?
You will see when we get there.

Nope, I think you've got the right question. Make your own call and defend it. But if you're using an inference provider for open weights, you're two API changes away from having no optionality at all. I'd rather own the stack and pay the frontier tax than rent a pipeline I can't debug.

Do frontier models have the same sort of degradation when the next model comes or arrives? I am seeing a similar inference provider: a response that meets certain prompting and configuration instructions. It's such a limited capability that models released one year back by frontier can still do the job. The only difference here is the economics, the token rates. The one I'm using is exceptionally cheap and gets the job done.

Of course I'm biased, go get your own opinion. The degradation pattern is the same on both sides. The difference is when the frontier model changes, I get a new capability I can decide to use or ignore. When your provider changes the open model under you, you get a silent regression and a re-tuning bill. The economics win now, but you're not pricing in the labor of chasing their updates.
